lead: Ray theory treats light in a fiber as straight lines that bend at boundaries by Snell's law. The core has a higher refractive index than the cladding, and a ray that meets the core–cladding boundary at a steep enough angle is reflected back completely: total internal reflection (TIR). Working backwards from that condition to the end face gives the acceptance angle, the half-angle of the cone of light a fiber can take in. The same reasoning sizes lenses and alignment when a source is coupled to a fiber.

sections.h3: Snell's law and the critical angle

blocks.text: The refractive index n of a material is the ratio of the speed of light in vacuum c to its speed v in the material: n = c/v. It has no unit; a larger n means slower light. In a step-index fiber the core index is n₁ and the cladding index is n₂, with n₁ > n₂. The medium outside the fiber end has index n₀ (air, n₀ = 1).

At a boundary, Snell's law links the angles on the two sides: n₁ sin θ₁ = n₂ sin θ₂. Both angles are measured from the normal, the line perpendicular to the boundary. The reflected ray leaves at the same angle as the incident ray (law of reflection).

Going from the denser core into the rarer cladding, the ray bends away from the normal, so θ₂ > θ₁. As θ₁ grows, θ₂ reaches 90° first: the refracted ray grazes the boundary. That value of θ₁ is the critical angle θc. Put θ₂ = 90° in Snell's law: n₁ sin θc = n₂.

blocks.where: θ<sub>c</sub> is measured from the normal at the core–cladding boundary; it exists only when n₁ > n₂.

blocks.text: For any angle of incidence above θc, Snell's law would need sin θ₂ > 1, which no real angle gives, so no light is transmitted and all of it is reflected back into the core. That is total internal reflection. Its two conditions are: light travels from the higher index to the lower index (n₁ > n₂), and the angle of incidence exceeds θc. Even then a weak evanescent field reaches a short way into the cladding, but it carries no power away.

sections.h3: From TIR at the wall to the acceptance angle

blocks.text: Take a meridional ray, one that passes through the fiber axis. It enters the flat end face from the outside medium at angle θ₀ to the axis. The end face is perpendicular to the axis, so the axis is its normal. Snell's law at the end face gives n₀ sin θ₀ = n₁ sin θr, where θr is the ray's angle to the axis inside the core.

The ray then meets the core–cladding wall. The wall runs parallel to the axis, so its normal is at right angles to the axis, and the angle of incidence on the wall is φ = 90° − θ<sub>r</sub>. TIR needs φ ≥ θ<sub>c</sub>, which means θ<sub>r</sub> ≤ 90° − θ<sub>c</sub>.
The acceptance angle θa is the largest outside angle θ₀ that still meets this, so at the limit θr = 90° − θc:

items: n₀ sin θ<sub>a</sub> = n₁ sin(90° − θ<sub>c</sub>) = n₁ cos θ<sub>c</sub>.
So n₀ sin θ<sub>a</sub> = n₁ √(1 − n₂²/n₁²) = √(n₁² − n₂²).

blocks.where: θa is the acceptance half-angle in the outside medium, measured from the fiber axis. The quantity n₀ sin θa is the numerical aperture, treated fully in Numerical aperture and skew rays.

blocks.text: Rotating θa about the axis sweeps out the acceptance cone. A meridional ray launched inside the cone (θ₀ < θa) meets the wall above θc and is guided; a ray launched outside it meets the wall below θc, loses part of its power into the cladding at every reflection and dies out within a short length.

The cone decides how much of a source's light enters the fiber. An LED spreads light over a wide angle, so only the part inside the cone is captured; a laser's narrow beam fits inside easily. A wider cone (larger n₁² − n₂²) collects more light, but the same index step also lets more modes travel, which spreads pulses (see Intermodal dispersion with signal degradation in fibers). Tilting the fiber end relative to the source moves part of the beam outside the cone, which is why angular misalignment costs power at joints.

This picture holds for meridional rays in a fiber whose core is many wavelengths wide. Rays that never cross the axis, called skew rays, follow helical paths and are accepted over a slightly wider cone; see Numerical aperture and skew rays. When the core is only a few wavelengths wide, rays give way to modes: Electromagnetic mode theory; modes in planar guides.

examples.question: A step-index fiber has core index n₁ = 1.50 and cladding index n₂ = 1.45, with air outside (n₀ = 1). Find the critical angle at the core–cladding boundary, the numerical aperture and the acceptance angle. Then find the ray angle inside the core for a ray launched exactly at the acceptance angle, and check that it meets the wall at θ<sub>c</sub>.
steps: Critical angle: sin θ<sub>c</sub> = n₂/n₁ = 1.45/1.50 = 0.9667, so θ<sub>c</sub> = sin⁻¹(0.9667) = 75.16°.
Squares: n₁² = 2.2500 and n₂² = 2.1025, so n₁² − n₂² = 0.1475.
Inside the core: sin θ<sub>r</sub> = sin θ<sub>a</sub>/n₁ = 0.3841/1.50 = 0.2560, so θ<sub>r</sub> = 14.84°.
Angle on the wall: φ = 90° − 14.84° = 75.16°, which equals θ<sub>c</sub>. The limiting ray just meets the TIR condition, as the derivation says.
examples.answer: θ<sub>c</sub> = 75.2°, NA = 0.384 and θ<sub>a</sub> = 22.6°; the limiting ray travels at 14.8° to the axis inside the core and strikes the wall at exactly 75.2°.

traps: Use sin θ<sub>c</sub> = n₂/n₁, not n₁/n₂; with n₂ < n₁ the ratio is below 1, as a sine must be.
Angles in Snell's law are measured from the normal. A ray 15° from the wall is 75° from the wall's normal.
θ<sub>c</sub> is inside the fiber at the core–cladding wall; θ<sub>a</sub> is outside, at the end face, measured from the axis. Do not call θ<sub>c</sub> the acceptance angle.
With a medium other than air at the end face, divide by n₀: sin θ<sub>a</sub> = √(n₁² − n₂²)/n₀. The cone in water is narrower than in air.
A ray launched at a larger angle hits the wall at a smaller angle of incidence (φ = 90° − θ<sub>r</sub>), so it is the steep launch that escapes, not the shallow one.

quiz.q: State the two conditions for total internal reflection at the core–cladding boundary.
quiz.a: Light must go from the higher-index core to the lower-index cladding (n₁ > n₂), and its angle of incidence, measured from the normal, must exceed the critical angle θ<sub>c</sub>.

quiz.q: Define a meridional ray and the critical angle.
quiz.a: A meridional ray passes through the fiber axis and stays in one plane. The critical angle is the angle of incidence at which the refracted ray grazes the boundary (θ₂ = 90°); sin θ<sub>c</sub> = n₂/n₁.

quiz.q: Why must the core index be higher than the cladding index?
quiz.a: Only when light goes into a lower index does it bend away from the normal, so that the refracted angle can reach 90° and a critical angle exists. If n₂ were larger, every ray would refract into the cladding and TIR could not trap it.

quiz.q: A fiber has n₁ = 1.48 and n₂ = 1.46 with air outside. Find θ<sub>c</sub>, NA and θ<sub>a</sub>.
The fiber of the worked example (n₁ = 1.50, n₂ = 1.45) is dipped in water, n₀ = 1.33. Find the acceptance angle in water.
quiz.a: sin θ<sub>a</sub> = 0.3841/1.33 = 0.2888, so θ<sub>a</sub> = 16.78°, smaller than 22.59° in air.

quiz.q: A meridional ray enters the worked example's fiber from air at 25° to the axis. Is it guided? Check it at the wall.
quiz.a: Inside: sin θ<sub>r</sub> = sin 25°/1.50 = 0.4226/1.50 = 0.2817, θ<sub>r</sub> = 16.36°. Wall angle φ = 90° − 16.36° = 73.64°, below θ<sub>c</sub> = 75.16°, so TIR fails and the ray leaks out. This agrees with 25° > θ<sub>a</sub> = 22.59°.

quiz.q: Why is the acceptance angle quoted outside the fiber rather than inside the core?
quiz.a: It describes the cone a source must launch into from the outside medium. Refraction at the end face shrinks the angle inside (22.59° outside becomes 14.84° inside in the worked example), so the inside angle is not the launch angle.

beyond: Not for the exam. Ray optics is accurate when the core is many wavelengths across, as in multimode and plastic optical fibers, light guides and endoscopes, and it is still how illumination optics and fiber sensors are designed. For single-mode fibers, with cores only a few wavelengths wide, mode theory replaces it. Search next for meridional ray tracing in step-index fiber, Goos–Hänchen shift and plastic optical fiber.

figure.caption: The worked example’s limiting ray: launched from air at θₐ = 22.6°, it bends to 14.8° inside the core and meets the wall at 90° − 14.8° = 75.2°, exactly the critical angle, so it is just reflected. A steeper launch would meet the wall below θ<sub>c</sub> and leak.
